Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target by shaping incoming waves accordingly. This paper demonstrates that a similar beneficial effect can be achieved even in the absence of system specifics, based solely on measured outgoing wave patterns, and establishes the relevant transformation (transfer matrix) that accurately reconstructs the internal distribution. This discovery holds potential for enhancing energy delivery in complex scattering environments determined experimentally.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section analysis for complex parameters, building upon the work of [arXiv:hep-ph-0411299] and [arXiv:arXiv:1006.5045], while bottom-quark annihilation contributions are calculated at tree level, addressing all possible processes involving exchange of scalar particles, pseudo-scalar particles, and mixtures thereof.

A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes a simulation-based correction for continuous models and an alternative method based on the work of Chandra and Sil (2018) for Poisson models. The proposed methods are applicable to a wide range of general network autoregressive models.

Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network architectures.

A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes.

The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific types of temporal cyclic transactions worthy of further law enforcement investigation, according to our survey of 1000 participants. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by detecting 13% more malicious transactions in the Ethereum blockchain than existing methods based on wallet address analysis alone.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy.

This paper explores the behavior of Smarandache's sequence from the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) at A061076, specifically focusing on its associated sequences, A061077 and A061078, linked to the Smarandache's sigma product of digits. We address open questions by identifying upper bounds applicable to all natural numbers 'n', as well as establishing that for sequences 'a(n)' and 'b(n)', there exists a number 'k' such that 'a(k)' equals 'b(k)'. Moreover, we establish that the inequality 10^n-1 divides evenly into (σ(n))^n for all natural numbers 'n'. Additionally, we present results related to modified sequences derived from OEIS sequences A061079, A061080, and A061081.

Cloud-based HPC deployments can provide cost savings and optimal resource allocation.
However, there are significant differences between the network architectures of cloud and on-premise HPC systems.
These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.
Initially, the investigation focuses on latency, bandwidth, and data transfer patterns in small-scale tests, followed by simulations on a larger scale.
Validation is conducted across multiple cloud providers and HPC systems, revealing that system noise and variability can substantially impact both performance and cost at both small and large scales.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound as if contexts were fully observable. This achievement is notable as it outperforms existing bounds by a significant margin. This achievement particularly occurred when the time horizon is substantial. When the distribution is known the approach offers an information theoretically optimal bound.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the existing literature reveal limitations under slower testing sample size growth. In contrast, the testing sample size requirement for DRITR is more relaxed than that of efficient policy evaluation using combined data. In Section 3, we emphasize the broad applicability and utility of DRITR.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.

This paper proposes the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform as a derivative of the Linear Canonical Transform, and proves related inequalities, including Heisenberg's Inequality and a logarithmic inequality for LCST.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses to examine the extremal gain of optimal power control in contrast to traditional fixed power allocation methods. We investigate how optimal power control impacts overall throughput in two main scenarios: (1) interference networks and (2) broadcast channels, focusing particularly on scenarios with multiple input and output streams. Our research reveals that in all mentioned scenarios with multiple input and output streams, the maximum achievable gain from using optimal power control, as opposed to fixed power allocation methods, grows at a rate proportional to the number of transmitting devices in the network. Consequently, this gain does not suffice to fully compensate for increased noise in wideband systems. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that under certain signal-to-noise ratio constraints, optimal power control can yield the maximum possible GDoF, thus confirming the extremal gain phenomenon previously proposed by Jindal in 2003. Notably, our research shows that in wideband systems with multiple input and output streams, the extremal gain of optimal power control is proportional to the number of transmitting devices in the network.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was integrated into the publicly accessible code "DNSsolver" on GitHub, along with a new simulation routine that prevents particle kinematic constraints from becoming stiff. We also validated our method for stretching collision time steps in simulations of turbulent flow with particles, revealing that stretching collision time steps by a factor of up to 64 maintains relatively minor deviations in particle distribution and sediment entrainment, although this may vary depending on flow conditions. However, we found that even small changes in stretching collision time steps can result in notable changes in turbulence, potentially affecting particle re-attachment and influencing overall simulation duration. Therefore, we recommend developing high-fidelity models with fine-grained collision time steps, even if this requires significant computational resources.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains.

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values.

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass.

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best current models (e.g., T5-Large and FLAN) manage only 42% accuracy on this dataset, highlighting a significant performance gap that motivates further research. You can find our dataset at https://github.com/ghrua/Condaqa.

Organizational structures known as information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify its comprehension. Although they are widely applied in various contexts such as taxonomy, menu navigation, report compilation, and database querying, the fundamental task of creating these structures from scratch remains understudied. In an effort to address this gap, we are introducing a novel task called information hierarchy construction (IHC), which involves automatically generating suitable structures for representing content across multiple levels of abstraction. To facilitate the development of effective IHC solutions, we have established a framework for evaluating and benchmarking different approaches, which includes both optimization-based and learning-based methods for constructing information hierarchies. To further enhance the quality of these structures, we have introduced an innovative process called interactive information hierarchy construction, which allows end-users to refine automatically generated structures in a data-driven and efficient manner.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that quenching can be employed to mimic annealing protocols, specifically those defined by Hamiltonian pathways $\lambda(p)$. By abruptly setting $\lambda$ to a extreme value (either $0$ or $\infinite$) within a Hamiltonian interlude, a quenching scenario can be created that emulates the annealing process for a given Hamiltonian path $\lambda(p)$. This allows for the application of quenching to replicate annealing outcomes, thereby sidestepping the gradual modification requirement while still yielding desirable solutions. As an example, we successfully solve a spin glass problem of $2^{14}$ variables, a challenge previously thought to be insurmountable for quantum annealing.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation
where the filled $s$-band becomes decoupled from the correlated $d$-band, with
the latter exhibiting itself-doped, $d$-wave pairing ground states when
antiferromagnetic order is suppressed.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes.

We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 300 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m, which takes into account solar radiation reflected off the water. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties that pinpoint potential discrepancies between observed wave behaviors and previous models at moderate wind speeds. Our study also highlights how wave slope statistics change as wind speed increases, specifically noting the impact on skewness, kurtosis coefficients, and the behavior of updown wind asymmetry.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, the abundance of opinions on the internet has created a significant challenge in identifying the majority viewpoint, prompting researchers to develop various methods for sentiment classification. This task becomes even more complicated due to the presence of slang language, which often poses an obstacle in understanding the underlying emotion. In an attempt to contribute to the efforts to manage the emotional impact of the pandemic, we have implemented a comprehensive study comprising three distinct aspects. Firstly, we have implemented a comparative analysis of multiple machine learning techniques, including Naive Bayes, decision trees, and neural networks, to establish the effectiveness of sentiment classification. Secondly, we have undertaken a comparative analysis of different feature extraction methods, combining them with a linguistic approach to determine the optimal technique. Thirdly, we have undertaken a thorough investigation of various sentiment classification approaches, including conventional machine learning, deep learning, and ensemble methods, to establish the optimal strategy. The findings of our comparative study have validated the superiority of the BERT model over other machine learning techniques, prompting us to introduce a custom-built dataset comprising Persian sentences.
